entries.name: Start here: the baseline
entries.summary: A new Windows PC to a working Linux development setup: WSL 2 with Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, Windows Terminal, zsh, uv, fnm and pnpm, kubectl, Terraform, the Azure CLI, Docker and Claude Code.

version.name: Baseline
version.docs: The tool pages linked from each tab, read 2026-10-29. The date is the WSL release.

notes: The split (WSL for development, Windows for the browser, games and Windows-only apps) is a choice, not a vendor recommendation. Microsoft's own guidance is to keep files on the same side as the tools that use them.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Windows keeps the browser, Office, games and anything Windows-only. Development happens in Ubuntu running in WSL 2: a real Linux userland, the same commands as the docs and as CI, and its ports reachable from the Windows browser on `localhost`.

items.alt: Windows 11 runs Windows Terminal and the browser. WSL 2 runs a lightweight VM with Ubuntu 26.04 inside. In Ubuntu the user's home holds the shell, runtimes, cluster and cloud tools, Docker Engine and the repositories. The browser reaches services in Ubuntu through localhost.
items.caption: What runs where.

cards.title: Linux first
cards.text: Docs, scripts and CI assume Linux. WSL runs them unmodified.

cards.title: Files in Linux
cards.text: Repositories live in `~/src`, not `/mnt/c`. Crossing file systems is slow.

cards.title: Your user, not root
cards.text: Install every per-user tool as your normal user. Check with `whoami`.

cards.title: You update it
cards.text: Windows does not upgrade the distribution. Run apt and the tool updaters yourself.

rows: Linux userland next to Windows apps. `localhostForwarding` is on by default, so a server in WSL opens in the Windows browser.
A VM that takes memory (half of Windows RAM by default). You maintain the distribution.
A separate Linux machine over SSH
Real hardware, good for long-running services and networking labs.
A second machine, and the browser on Windows reaches services only over the network.
Linux-first docs and scripts need translating. Package managers: winget or Scoop.
items.caption: The judgement is this page's; the facts in the WSL row come from the WSL settings page.

sections.title: The order
sections.intro: Each line is a tab on this page.

items: Windows: run `wsl --install` in an admin PowerShell, reboot, create the Linux user. [WSL and Ubuntu](#wsl)
Windows: make Windows Terminal the default terminal and Ubuntu the default profile. [Terminal](#windows-terminal)
Ubuntu: `sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade`, check `/etc/wsl.conf` (systemd, default user), set `.wslconfig` limits on Windows.
Ubuntu: `git config --global user.name` and `user.email`, before any commit. [Git and Claude Code](#claude-code)
Ubuntu: install zsh, make it the login shell, add the plugins and the prompt. [Shell](#zsh)
Ubuntu: Claude Code. [Git and Claude Code](#claude-code)
Ubuntu: uv for Python. [Python](#uv)
Ubuntu: fnm for Node, then pnpm. [Node](#node)
Ubuntu: kubectl and the cluster tools. [Kubernetes](#kubectl)
Ubuntu: Terraform (or OpenTofu) and the Azure CLI. [Terraform](#terraform), [Azure CLI](#azure-cli)
Ubuntu: Docker Engine, then kind for a local cluster. [Containers](#docker)

sections.title: Rules that save time

items.title: Never install a user tool as root
items.text: uv, fnm, pnpm, starship and Claude Code install into the current user's home (`~/.local/bin`, `~/.local/share`). Run as root by mistake, they land in `/root` and your user does not see them. If WSL starts as root, set `[user] default=<name>` in `/etc/wsl.conf`.

items: Use `sudo` only for apt and for files under `/etc`. Never `sudo npm` or `sudo pip`.
Ubuntu's `python3` belongs to the system. PEP 668 marks it externally managed, so `pip install` outside a virtual environment is refused. Use uv.
Prefer the vendor's apt repository (kubectl, Terraform, Azure CLI, Docker) over a downloaded binary: `apt upgrade` then updates it.

rows: Ubuntu packages and the apt repositories (kubectl, terraform, az, docker)
kubectl to a new minor version
Change the version in `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list`, then apt
Updates itself in the background; `claude doctor` shows the last attempt
The Microsoft Store updates it; a GitHub install does not update itself

items.title: Free the memory
items.text: `wsl --shutdown` stops every distribution and the WSL 2 VM. `wsl --terminate <distro>` stops only one.

entries.name: WSL and Ubuntu
entries.summary: Windows Subsystem for Linux 2 runs a Linux distribution in a lightweight VM. Install it with one command, with Ubuntu 26.04 LTS, then tune it with /etc/wsl.conf and %UserProfile%\.wslconfig.

version.name: WSL
version.docs: learn.microsoft.com/windows/wsl (no version on the pages); Ubuntu 26.04.1 LTS from documentation.ubuntu.com/wsl

notes: The pages read give no WSL version. 3.0.3 is the latest GitHub release that is not a prerelease; 3.0.4 (2026-10-20) is a prerelease.
Ubuntu 26.04 release date: the image files on releases.ubuntu.com are dated 2026-04-23 (unconfirmed as the announcement date).
Microsoft documents systemd as off by default in wsl.conf; whether the Ubuntu 26.04 image turns it on was not stated on the pages read (unconfirmed). Check the file.
Some games' anti-cheat may object to the hypervisor WSL 2 needs (unconfirmed, not on the pages read).

sections.title: In one minute
items: WSL 2 runs Linux distributions in a lightweight utility VM managed by Windows. `wsl --install` enables the features and installs Ubuntu by default. New installs use WSL 2.

Two config files: `/etc/wsl.conf` inside each distribution (systemd, default user, automount, interop) and `%UserProfile%\.wslconfig` on Windows for the VM (memory, processors, networking). Changes apply after the VM stops: `wsl --shutdown`, or wait about 8 seconds after closing every shell.
The `Ubuntu` distribution always tracks the latest LTS, today 26.04 LTS (Resolute Raccoon). `Ubuntu-26.04` pins that release. Interim releases are not offered on WSL.

sections.title: Install WSL and Ubuntu
sections.intro: In PowerShell run as administrator, then reboot. Needs Windows 10 2004 (build 19041) or later, or Windows 11, and virtualisation on in the firmware.

items.title: Install WSL with the default distribution
Or pick a release from the list

items: `wsl --install Ubuntu-26.04` installs that release. If the download hangs at 0.0%, add `--web-download`.
On first start Ubuntu asks for a Linux user name and password. They are not your Windows account; this user is the distribution's administrator (`sudo`).

sections.title: First commands in Ubuntu

items.title: Update the packages

source.label: Set up a WSL development environment

items.match: sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade

items: Windows does not update or upgrade the distribution. Run this regularly.
Make a home for code in the Linux file system, for example `mkdir ~/src`. `explorer.exe .` opens the current directory in File Explorer; from Windows the path is `\\wsl$\<distro>\home\<user>`.

items.title: Keep repositories out of /mnt/c
items.text: Files under `/mnt/c` are on Windows and every access crosses file systems, which is much slower for Linux tools (git, node, Claude Code's search). Microsoft recommends storing files on the side of the tools that use them.

sections.title: wsl.conf: systemd and the default user
sections.intro: Edit with `sudo nano /etc/wsl.conf`, then `wsl --shutdown` from PowerShell.
items: Microsoft's systemd page shows snap and microk8s on WSL; Docker Engine runs as a systemd service. Check with `systemctl list-unit-files --type=service`. Ubuntu recommends keeping systemd and interop on.
Default user: `[user]` then `default=<name>`. The old `ubuntu config --default-user <name>` needs the distribution's .exe launcher, which the new tar-based (.wsl) images do not have, so use wsl.conf.
Other keys: `[interop] appendWindowsPath=false` keeps Windows' PATH out of Linux; `[network] generateResolvConf=false` lets you write your own `/etc/resolv.conf`.

sections.title: .wslconfig: memory, processors, networking
sections.intro: In `%UserProfile%\.wslconfig` on Windows. WSL Settings in the Start menu edits the same values.

rows: `mirrored` (Windows 11 22H2+): Windows and Linux share interfaces, both reach each other on `127.0.0.1`, IPv6 works. Microsoft recommends trying it, and it can help with VPNs.
Ports opened in WSL are reachable on Windows `localhost`. Ignored in mirrored mode.
The VM stops after this idle time (Windows 11).
`gradual` returns cached memory to Windows slowly instead of at once; `disabled` turns it off.
New virtual disks are sparse and give space back.
List distributions, their state and WSL version.
Stop every distribution and the VM. Frees the memory and applies config changes.
Update WSL from the Microsoft Store (`--web-download` for GitHub).
Open as root, for example to reset a forgotten password with `passwd <user>`.

sections.title: Reference
items: The Ubuntu `Ubuntu` app is upgraded to a new LTS once its first point release ships; numbered apps such as `Ubuntu-26.04` stay on that release with five years of standard support.
cloud-init can pre-configure a new instance from `%UserProfile%\.cloud-init\<distro>.user-data`. It runs once, on first start, and needs systemd and interop.
`[boot] command=` runs a command as root when the distribution starts (Windows 11). `[automount] options` sets permissions for Windows drives under `/mnt`.

entries.name: zsh
entries.summary: The recommended interactive shell here: bash-like syntax, the best completion support across the tools on this page, and plugins for suggestions and highlighting from Ubuntu's archive.

version.name: zsh
version.docs: Ubuntu 26.04 package 5.9-8ubuntu3. Upstream is at 5.9.2 (2026-07-12) per zsh.org news.

compare.text: fish has suggestions and highlighting built in but is not POSIX compatible, so copied bash snippets often fail. zsh runs most of them.
Oh My Zsh is a framework of plugins and themes on top of zsh. This page uses two plugins from apt and Starship instead, which is less to load and update.

notes: "Best shell" is a judgement: zsh is chosen because every tool here documents zsh completion (kubectl, uv, fnm, fzf, zoxide, starship) and bash snippets from docs mostly work in it. bash stays the system shell for scripts.
The licence is zsh's own LICENCE file: a permissive licence, with some shell functions under GPL versions per that file. The first release date was not checked.
The Azure CLI's completion under zsh was not described on the pages read (unconfirmed).

sections.title: In one minute
items: zsh is designed for interactive use and took many features of bash, ksh and tcsh. Ubuntu's default login shell is bash; this step makes zsh the login shell for your user only. Scripts keep their own `#!/bin/bash` line and are unaffected.

cards.title: Starship
cards.text: A fast prompt showing git branch, Kubernetes context, Python and Node versions.

cards.title: Suggestions and highlighting
cards.text: zsh-autosuggestions and zsh-syntax-highlighting, both from apt.

cards.title: fzf and zoxide
cards.text: Fuzzy history search (`Ctrl+R`) and `z <dir>` to jump.

sections.title: Install zsh and make it the login shell
items: Use `sudo apt install zsh`.
Close every Ubuntu tab and open a new one (or `wsl --terminate Ubuntu`). `echo $SHELL` shows `/usr/bin/zsh`. The first start offers a setup menu; `0` creates an empty `~/.zshrc`.

sections.title: Plugins from apt
items: `sudo apt install zsh-autosuggestions zsh-syntax-highlighting` (Ubuntu 26.04: 0.7.1 and 0.8.0).
Add `source /usr/share/zsh-autosuggestions/zsh-autosuggestions.zsh` to `~/.zshrc` (the path is the Debian package's).

items.title: Order matters
items.text: zsh-syntax-highlighting must be the last plugin sourced, at the end of `~/.zshrc`. Its authors recommend this manual setup over a plugin manager.

sections.title: Prompt, fuzzy search, jumping
items: Starship needs a Nerd Font in the terminal for its icons.
`sudo apt install fzf zoxide` (Ubuntu 26.04: fzf 0.67.0, zoxide 0.9.8).
`--zsh` exists from fzf 0.48.0; older versions source files from the package's `shell` directory instead.

sections.title: Completions for the tools on this page
sections.intro: Lines for `~/.zshrc`, each from the tool's own docs. Put them after `autoload -Uz compinit && compinit`.

sections.title: Reference
items: `~/.zshrc` is read by interactive shells. Tool installers that append to `~/.bashrc` (fnm, pnpm, uv when run from bash) must be repeated for zsh or their line copied over.
`exec zsh` reloads the shell after editing `~/.zshrc`.

entries.name: Python with uv
entries.summary: Astral's Python package and project manager. It installs Python versions, creates a .venv per project from pyproject.toml and uv.lock, and runs tools without installing them.
notes: Releases come several times a week; the page's commands rarely change between them.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Ubuntu's `python3` belongs to the system, and PEP 668 makes `pip install` outside a virtual environment fail. uv keeps everything in your home and in each project.

rows: uv itself, Python executables, tool commands

items: The cache should be on the same file system as the virtual environments, one more reason to keep projects in `~/src`.

sections.title: Install
items: Update with `uv self update`. A uv on Windows is a separate install (`winget install --id=astral-sh.uv -e`).

sections.title: A project
items: `uv run <cmd>` runs in the project environment after checking the lockfile is current; no `activate` needed. `uv sync` rebuilds `.venv` from `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`.
`uv python pin 3.13` writes `.python-version`. uv downloads a missing Python on its own when a command needs it.

items.title: What to commit
items.text: Commit `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock` and `.python-version`. Do not edit `uv.lock` by hand, and leave `.venv` out of git (`uv init` writes a .gitignore).

sections.title: Tools
items: `uvx ruff check .` runs a tool in a throwaway environment. `uvx` is the same as `uv tool run`.
`uv tool install ruff` installs it for good, in its own environment, with the command in `~/.local/bin`.

sections.title: Reference
items: Locations follow XDG: `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/uv`, `$XDG_DATA_HOME/uv`, `$XDG_BIN_HOME`. `uv cache dir` and `uv python dir` print them.
Installed as root by mistake, uv and its data are under `/root/.local` and `/root/.cache`: remove them and reinstall as your user.

sources.label: PEP 668: Marking Python base environments as externally managed

entries.name: Node.js with fnm
entries.summary: fnm (Fast Node Manager) installs Node.js versions in your home and switches them per directory from .node-version or .nvmrc. Node 26 is the current LTS. pnpm is the package manager.

version.name: fnm
version.docs: fnm README and docs/commands.md on GitHub; Node v26.13.0 LTS (2026-10-28) from nodejs.org

compare.text: mise manages Node, Python and many CLIs from one mise.toml. fnm does Node only.

notes: Whether fnm's installer writes `--use-on-cd` into the shell file was not stated in the README (unconfirmed). Installing with `--skip-shell` and adding the README's line avoids the question.
Corepack is not shipped with Node.js 25 and later, so `corepack enable pnpm` does not work on Node 26 unless Corepack is installed separately.

sections.title: In one minute
items: Ubuntu's Node package lags and global installs need sudo. fnm puts each Node version in your home and changes version when you `cd` into a project.
Node.js 26 is LTS (v26.13.0 on 2026-10-28); 24 (Krypton) and 22 (Jod) are still LTS. From Node 27 releases are yearly and every major version becomes LTS after six months as Current.

sections.title: Install fnm and Node

items.title: Install without touching the shell files

items: `fnm install --lts` installs the latest LTS. `fnm default <version>` sets the version used outside projects. fnm lives in `~/.local/share/fnm`.
Rerun the same install command to upgrade fnm.

sections.title: Per project
items: `node --version > .node-version` pins the version; `.nvmrc` works too. With `--use-on-cd`, entering the directory switches Node.

items.title: No sudo, no global project tools
items.text: Never `sudo npm`. A global `npm install -g` belongs to one Node version and disappears when you switch. Put project tools in devDependencies and run them through the package manager.

sections.title: pnpm
items: pnpm 12 is a native executable and runs without Node.js once installed.
Update with `pnpm self-update`. In a project, set `"packageManager": "pnpm@<version>"` in package.json; inside such a project `self-update` only updates that pin.
`pnx <pkg>` (alias `pnpm dlx`) runs a package without adding it, like `npx` or `uvx`.

sections.title: Reference
items: Upgrading fnm: rerun the installer with `--skip-shell` to avoid a second loader in the shell file.
`fnm list-remote --lts` lists LTS versions. The `--corepack-enabled` option (or `FNM_COREPACK_ENABLED`) makes fnm call `corepack enable` on every Node install, where Corepack exists.

items.title: One minor version per repository
items.text: The repository URL names a minor version (`v1.37`). `apt upgrade` brings patches only. For the next minor, change the version in `/etc/apt/sources.list.d/kubernetes.list`, then `apt-get update` and `upgrade`.

items: `kubectl version --client` checks the install. An alias such as `k` gets the same completion.

sections.title: Helm and the helpers
items: Helm also has a community apt repository hosted by Buildkite (on the same page). Helm 3 still gets releases (v3.22.1 on 2026-10-15).
k9s: download the `.deb` from its releases and `sudo apt install ./k9s_linux_amd64.deb`, as its README shows.
kubectx and kubens: `sudo apt install kubectx`.

sections.title: A local cluster with kind
items: `kind create cluster` creates a cluster; its kubectl context is `kind-kind`. `kind delete cluster` removes it.

sections.title: kubeadm on a workstation?
items: kubeadm bootstraps cluster nodes. It needs a container runtime and kubelet on every machine, 2 GB of RAM and 2 CPUs for a control plane, and kubelet fails on swap unless configured. It does not install kubelet or kubectl for you.
Learn it on VMs or a homelab; for daily development a kind cluster is faster and disposable. Install kubeadm only where you build nodes.

entries.summary: Set git's name and email, then install Claude Code inside WSL with Anthropic's native installer. Claude Code needs a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise) or a Console account.
notes: Claude Code is not open source; its licence refers to Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service. It is here because it is part of the workflow this topic sets up.
Whether Claude Code's Chrome integration works from inside WSL was not described on the pages read (unconfirmed).
If login does not open a browser from WSL, copying the printed URL into the Windows browser is common practice (unconfirmed on the pages read).

sections.title: Git first
items: Ubuntu 26.04 ships git 2.53.0 (`sudo apt install git` if missing).

items.title: Name and email, once per machine
Do it before the first commit
items.text: A new Ubuntu has no git identity. `git commit` then stops with "Author identity unknown ... Please tell me who you are" and `fatal: empty ident name`. Set both values once with `--global`; `git config --global --list` shows them. Run it as your own user: root has its own `~/.gitconfig`.

items: Credentials: install Git for Windows and WSL's git can use Git Credential Manager, which stores tokens in the Windows Credential Manager. Or use SSH keys in `~/.ssh`. GCM only works with HTTPS remotes.

sections.title: Install Claude Code in WSL
sections.intro: In the Ubuntu shell, not PowerShell. WSL 2 supports Claude Code's sandboxing; WSL 1 does not.
items: Open a new shell and run `claude --version`, then `claude` to log in. The launcher is `~/.local/bin/claude`, a link into `~/.local/share/claude/versions/`.
`claude doctor` prints install health, settings errors and the last update attempt.

items.title: Updates
items.text: The native install updates itself in the background. The `autoUpdatesChannel` setting picks `latest` (default) or `stable` (typically about a week old, skipping releases with major regressions). apt, Homebrew and WinGet installs do not update themselves.

sections.title: Working well in WSL
items: Keep projects under `/home`, not `/mnt/c`: across file systems Claude Code's search can return fewer results.
An npm package also exists; never install it with `sudo npm install -g`.
A project's `CLAUDE.md` can state the toolchain: `uv run` and `uv add` instead of pip, pnpm for Node.

entries.name: Starship
entries.summary: A fast, cross-shell prompt written in Rust: git, Kubernetes context, language versions.

sections.title: What it is
items: Install with its script or a package manager, then `eval "$(starship init zsh)"` at the end of `~/.zshrc`. Needs a Nerd Font. Configured in `~/.config/starship.toml`.

entries.name: fzf
entries.summary: A general-purpose command-line fuzzy finder with key bindings for history (Ctrl+R), files (Ctrl+T) and directories (Alt+C).

sections.title: What it is
items: `sudo apt install fzf`, then `source <(fzf --zsh)` in `~/.zshrc` (fzf 0.48.0 and later). Setting `FZF_CTRL_R_COMMAND=` and friends to empty disables a binding.

entries.name: zoxide
entries.summary: A smarter cd: `z <part of a path>` jumps to the most used matching directory.

sections.title: What it is
items: `sudo apt install zoxide`, then `eval "$(zoxide init zsh)"` at the end of `~/.zshrc`.

entries.name: Oh My Zsh
entries.summary: A community framework for zsh configuration with 300+ plugins and 140+ themes.

version.name: Oh My Zsh
version.docs: GitHub README read on the check date; the project publishes no releases

notes: No releases, so there is no version to track: the README date is the version.

sections.title: What it is
items: Installs with a script into `~/.oh-my-zsh` and rewrites `~/.zshrc`. Plugins are listed in `plugins=(...)`. An alternative to the hand-made setup on the Shell tab, with more to load.

entries.name: fish
entries.summary: A friendly shell with suggestions, highlighting and completions built in. Intentionally not POSIX compatible.
notes: GitHub reports the licence as NOASSERTION; the COPYING file was not read beyond its header.

sections.title: What it is
items: Works well out of the box, but it is intentionally not POSIX compatible: bash syntax such as `[[` does not work, so snippets from docs need translating. kubectl, uv, fnm and fzf all support fish.

sources.label: fish docs: Fish for bash users

entries.name: pnpm
entries.summary: A fast Node.js package manager with a shared content-addressed store. pnpm 12 is a native executable.

sections.title: What it is
items: Install with `curl -fsSL https://get.pnpm.io/install.sh | sh -`; update with `pnpm self-update`. pnpm 10, 11 and 12 support Node 22 to 26. `pnx` (alias `pnpm dlx`) runs a package without installing it.

entries.name: mise
entries.summary: One tool to install and switch versions of Node, Python, kubectl, Terraform and more per project, plus env vars and tasks, from mise.toml.
notes: Releases come almost daily, so `make check` will often list it.

sections.title: What it is
items: `curl -fsSL https://mise.run | sh` puts `mise` in `~/.local/bin`. `mise use node@24` installs and records the version in `mise.toml`. An alternative to fnm and uv's Python management when one file for every tool matters more.

entries.name: kubeadm
entries.summary: The Kubernetes tool to bootstrap cluster nodes. Not needed on a workstation that only talks to clusters.

cncf.text: Kubernetes was accepted to CNCF on March 10, 2016 at the Incubating maturity level and moved to Graduated on March 6, 2018.

compare.text: kind runs a whole cluster in Docker with one command; kubeadm sets up real nodes.

sections.title: What it is
items: Installed with kubelet and kubectl from the same pkgs.k8s.io repository on every node. Needs 2 GB RAM, 2 CPUs on a control plane, a container runtime, and swap off or tolerated by kubelet.

entries.name: Helm
entries.summary: The Kubernetes package manager. Helm 4 is current; Helm 3 still gets releases.

cncf.text: Helm was accepted to CNCF on June 1, 2018 at the Incubating maturity level and moved to Graduated on May 1, 2020.

sections.title: What it is
items: Install with the `get-helm-4` script or the community apt repository. Charts, values and commands are covered in [GitOps: Helm](../gitops/index.html#helm).

entries.name: kind
entries.summary: Kubernetes IN Docker: local clusters whose nodes are Docker containers.

cncf.text: A Kubernetes SIG project (kubernetes-sigs), not listed as its own CNCF project.

sections.title: What it is
items: Needs Docker, Podman or nerdctl. Download the binary from the quick start, then `kind create cluster`. Still pre-1.0.

entries.name: k9s
entries.summary: A terminal UI to watch and manage a Kubernetes cluster.

sections.title: What it is
items: On Ubuntu: download `k9s_linux_amd64.deb` from the latest release and `sudo apt install ./k9s_linux_amd64.deb`. It uses the current kubectl context.

entries.name: kubectx and kubens
entries.summary: Switch kubectl contexts (kubectx) and namespaces (kubens) quickly.

sections.title: What it is
items: `sudo apt install kubectx` installs both. Also available as krew plugins `ctx` and `ns`.

entries.name: krew
entries.summary: The plugin manager for kubectl.

cncf.text: A Kubernetes SIG project (kubernetes-sigs), not listed as its own CNCF project.

sections.title: What it is
items: Plugins install as `kubectl <name>`, for example `kubectl krew install ctx`. Needs kubectl 1.12 or later.

entries.name: kubelogin (Azure)
entries.summary: A client-go credential (exec) plugin for Azure authentication, used by AKS clusters with Microsoft Entra ID.

sections.title: What it is
items: `az aks install-cli` installs kubectl and kubelogin; or copy a release binary onto the PATH. Supported with kubectl 1.11 and later.

entries.name: OpenTofu
entries.summary: The open source fork of Terraform (MPL-2.0), a CNCF sandbox project. The command is `tofu`.

cncf.text: OpenTofu was accepted to CNCF on April 23, 2025 at the Sandbox maturity level.

compare.text: Terraform is BUSL-1.1 since 1.6; OpenTofu stays open source.

sections.title: What it is
items: Install from its apt repository at packages.opentofu.org, or with its installer script and `--install-method deb`.

entries.name: TFLint
entries.summary: A pluggable Terraform linter. The Terraform language ruleset is bundled; AWS, Azure and Google Cloud rulesets are plugins.

sections.title: What it is
items: On Linux, download `tflint_linux_amd64.zip` from the latest release and unzip it onto the PATH.

entries.name: Docker Desktop
entries.summary: Docker's Windows app; its WSL 2 backend runs the engine in WSL. Free for personal use, education and small businesses; a paid subscription otherwise.

version.name: Docker Desktop
version.docs: docs.docker.com WSL 2 backend and licence pages, read on the check date (no version on the pages)

compare.text: Docker Engine in Ubuntu is free and command line only.

notes: Prices and limits are the vendor's and change; read the licence page before relying on them.

sections.title: What it is
items: Free for small businesses (fewer than 250 employees and less than $10 million annual revenue), personal use and education. Larger organisations need Pro, Team or Business. Uninstall any Docker Engine inside WSL first: both together conflict. Terms change; check the licence page.

sections.title: What it is
items: Set `user.name` and `user.email` with `git config --global`. In WSL, Git Credential Manager from Git for Windows stores HTTPS tokens in the Windows Credential Manager.
